steps.intro: Notice where each word is stressed (the capitals), and listen for the dot that doubles a letter.

cards.title: Syllables
body: Every Hebrew syllable starts with a consonant and has one vowel. An open syllable ends with its vowel (דָּ in דָּבָר); a closed one ends with a consonant (מִשְׁ in מִשְׁפָּט).
To split a long word, work from the end: each vowel takes the consonant before it, and a silent shewa closes the syllable it sits in.

cards.title: Where the stress falls
body: Most words are stressed on the last syllable: da-VAR, mish-PAT, sha-LOM.
Some common nouns are stressed on the one before: words with two e-vowels like מֶלֶךְ (ME-lekh) and לֶחֶם (LE-chem), and the -ayim words like מַיִם (MA-yim) and שָׁמַיִם (sha-MA-yim).
In the Bible text most words also carry a small accent mark, which shows the stress and works like punctuation. The two strongest: ׃ ends a verse, and ֑ marks its middle.

cards.title: The dot that doubles, and the joining line
body: You met the dot that makes ב כ פ hard. The same dot after a vowel means the letter is doubled: in הַשָּׁמַיִם the שּׁ counts twice, hash-sha-, though in everyday reading it sounds like one. Grammar books call this dagesh forte (doubling) and the other dagesh lene (hard sound).
How to tell them apart: in ב ג ד כ פ ת at the start of a word or after a silent shewa, the dot just makes the sound hard. After a vowel, it doubles.
A short line at the top, ־, joins two words to be said as one, the first losing its stress: כָּל־הָאָרֶץ, kol ha-A-rets. It's called maqqef.

examples.en: after a vowel: ת is doubled
after a silent shewa: פּ is just hard (p)

cards.prompt: How many syllables does מִשְׁפָּט (justice) have?
cards.explain: Two vowels, two syllables: mish-PAT. The shewa under שׁ is silent.

cards.prompt: Which syllable is stressed in מֶלֶךְ (king)?
cards.explain: Nouns with two e-vowels like מֶלֶךְ are stressed on the first syllable.

cards.prompt: What does the dot in the שּׁ of הַשָּׁמַיִם show?
cards.explain: It follows a vowel (ַ), so it doubles the letter. ש isn't one of ב ג ד כ פ ת anyway.

cards.prompt: Match each mark to its job.
Describe the dot in the פּ of מִשְׁפָּט.
cards.explain: After a silent shewa, a dot in ב ג ד כ פ ת only makes the sound hard: mish-PAT.

cards.prompt: Split מִשְׁפָּט into its two syllables, from the right.

steps.intro: Read word by word: find each vowel, split the syllables, then put the stress where the capitals show.

cards.note: כַּמַּיִם (like the waters) has a doubled מּ, and מִשְׁפָּט (justice) follows: “Let justice roll down like waters.”
Find הָאָרֶץ, the earth, and the ׃ at the end of the verse.
